name: THVD1450DR
title: RS-485 transceivers, 3 V to 5.5 V supply, ±18 kV IEC ESD on the bus pins
summary: A family of four RS-485/RS-422 transceivers on one 3 V to 5.5 V supply, with bus pins rated ±18 kV IEC 61000-4-2 contact, ±25 kV air-gap and ±4 kV IEC 61000-4-4 burst, which removes the need for further system-level ESD and EFT protection parts. THVD1410 (500 kbps) and THVD1450 (50 Mbps) are half duplex with DE and RE; THVD1451 is full duplex with both halves always on; THVD1452 is full duplex with DE and RE. Each is an eighth of a unit load, works over ±15 V common mode, fails safe high on an open, shorted or idle bus, and is specified from -40 °C to 125 °C.

circuits.title: Half-duplex node protected against 1 kV surge
circuits.description: A 5 V half-duplex node protected against 1 kV IEC 61000-4-5 surge. One controller line, DIR, drives RE and DE together and has a 10 kΩ pull-down to ground; RxD has a 10 kΩ pull-up to 5 V. Each bus pin reaches the connector through a 10 Ω pulse-proof resistor, and a two-line bidirectional TVS clamps both connector lines to ground. Two 100 nF capacitors decouple the 5 V rail.

parts.note: bidirectional 400 W two-line TVS; IO1 and IO2 clamp to the common GND pin

circuits.title: Full-duplex node protected against 1 kV surge
circuits.description: The full-duplex version of the protected node, on 5 V. The controller has two DIR lines: one drives RE, the other drives DE, which has a 10 kΩ pull-down to ground. RxD has 10 kΩ to 5 V. Each of the four bus pins passes through a 10 Ω pulse-proof resistor to its connector, the A/B pair to one connector and the Y/Z pair to another, and each pair has its own two-line TVS to ground. One 100 nF capacitor decouples the 5 V rail.

circuits.title: RS-485 network of half-duplex transceivers
circuits.description: Four half-duplex transceivers hang in parallel on one twisted pair, every A on one wire and every B on the other. The nodes at the two ends of the cable each put a resistor RT, equal to the cable impedance, across the pair; the two nodes between them tap on with no termination.

circuits.title: RS-485 network of full-duplex transceivers
circuits.description: A master and two slaves on two twisted pairs. The master's Y/Z driver feeds the first pair, which every slave receives on A/B; the slaves' Y/Z drivers share the second pair, which the master receives on A/B. Each pair is terminated by RT at both ends, at the master and at the far slave; the middle slave taps both pairs unterminated.

circuits.title: Driver differential output voltage with common-mode load
circuits.description: DE is tied to VCC and D held at 0 V or VCC. RL spans A/Y to B/Z and VOD is read across it; a 375 Ω resistor from each output meets at the test source Vtest, referred to ground. The characteristics use RL = 60 Ω and Vtest from -15 V to 15 V. On the full-duplex parts Y stands in for A and Z for B.

circuits.title: Driver differential and common-mode output with RS-485 load
circuits.description: D is held at 0 V or VCC. Two RL/2 resistors in series span A/Y and B/Z; VOD is read across the pair and VOC from their midpoint, which also carries CL to ground. VOC(PP) is the peak-to-peak swing of VOC at the edges and ΔVOC(SS) the shift in its settled level. On the full-duplex parts Y stands in for A and Z for B.

circuits.title: Driver differential output rise and fall times and propagation delays
circuits.description: DE is tied to VCC. The generator drives D across a 50 Ω termination; A/Y and B/Z carry RL = 54 Ω and CL = 50 pF in parallel. Delays run from VI at 50 % to VOD at 50 %; rise and fall run between 10 % and 90 % of VOD, which swings about ±2 V. On the full-duplex parts Y stands in for A and Z for B.

circuits.title: Driver enable and disable times, active-high output with pull-down load
circuits.description: The generator drives DE across 50 Ω, D sets which output goes high, and switch S1 takes that output (A/Y or B/Z) as VO, loaded by CL = 50 pF and RL = 110 Ω to ground. tPZH runs from VI at 50 % to VO at 50 %; tPHZ from VI at 50 % to VO at 90 % of VOH. On the full-duplex parts Y stands in for A and Z for B.

circuits.title: Driver enable and disable times, active-low output with pull-up load
circuits.description: The generator drives DE across 50 Ω, D sets which output goes low, and S1 takes that output as VO, pulled to VCC by RL = 110 Ω and loaded by CL = 50 pF to ground. tPZL runs from VI at 50 % to VO at 50 %; tPLZ from VI at 50 % to VO 10 % above VOL. On the full-duplex parts Y stands in for A and Z for B.

circuits.title: Receiver output rise and fall times and propagation delays
circuits.description: The generator, swinging 0 V to 3 V, drives A across 50 Ω while B sits at 1.5 V and RE at 0 V. R drives CL = 15 pF to ground. Delays run from VI at 50 % to VO at 50 %; rise and fall between 10 % and 90 %.

parts.value: input generator, 50 Ω output, 0 V to 3 V

circuits.title: Receiver enable and disable times with driver enabled
circuits.description: DE is tied to VCC and D held at 0 V or VCC, so the part's own driver sets the bus. The generator drives RE across 50 Ω. R drives CL = 15 pF to ground and 1 kΩ to S1, which goes to ground when D is at VCC and to VCC when D is at 0 V. tPZH(1) and tPZL(1) run from VI at 50 % to VO at 50 %; tPHZ ends at 90 % of VOH and tPLZ 10 % above VOL.

circuits.title: Receiver enable times with driver disabled
circuits.description: With the driver off, A and B are held at 1.5 V and 0 V (S1 to ground) or at 0 V and 1.5 V (S1 to VCC). The generator drives RE across 50 Ω; R drives CL = 15 pF to ground and 1 kΩ to S1. tPZH(2) and tPZL(2) run from VI at 50 % to VO at 50 %.

operation.text: THVD1410 and THVD1450 are the same half-duplex transceiver in two speed grades, 500 kbps and 50 Mbps. THVD1451 is full duplex with no enable pins: driver and receiver are on whenever powered. THVD1452 is full duplex with a high-true driver enable and a low-true receiver enable. Turning both driver and receiver off brings supply current under 1 µA.
The typical differential output is larger than on older transceivers, for noise margin. With VCC at 5 V ±10 % the minimum |VOD| is 2.1 V, enough for PROFIBUS.

Protection on the bus pins takes IEC 61000-4-2 discharges up to ±18 kV and IEC 61000-4-4 fast transients up to ±4 kV. With care in the system design, ±4 kV EFT can be met to criterion A, with no data lost while the burst is present.

The receiver thresholds are biased inside the part so that both sit below 0 V differential, with large hysteresis. An open bus (a connector pulled), a shorted pair, or an idle bus that nobody drives all give a differential input near zero, which is above VTH+, so R stays high and no external failsafe bias resistors are needed. RS-422 and RS-485 require a high output above +200 mV and a low below -200 mV, and the threshold limits meet both. Near zero input, the output only goes low once the input falls more than VHYS below VTH+, so the noise margin during a bus fault is VTH+ plus the hysteresis.

With DE high, A follows D and B is its complement: D high drives A high and B low, giving positive VOD. With DE low both outputs are high impedance and D is ignored. DE has an internal pull-down, so an open DE leaves the driver off; D has an internal pull-up, so an open D with the driver on drives A high and B low.
With RE low the receiver is on: R is high when VID is above VTH+, low when it is below VTH-, and undefined between them. With RE high or open, R is high impedance.

Driver and receiver are permanently enabled. D high drives Y high and Z low (VOD = VY – VZ positive); D low reverses them. An open D is pulled up inside, so Y goes high and Z low. The receiver works as on the half-duplex parts and fails safe high on an open, shorted or idle bus.

Works like THVD1450 with the driver on separate pins: DE high lets D drive Y (and Z in complement), DE low or open puts Y and Z in high impedance, an open D drives Y high. RE low enables the receiver on A and B; RE high or open makes R high impedance.

Every transceiver connects in parallel to the bus cable. Each end of the cable carries a resistor RT equal to the cable's characteristic impedance Z0, which stops reflections and supports higher rates over longer runs. A full-duplex link uses two pairs, so each node can send on one pair while receiving on the other.

Cable length and data rate trade against each other. Typical RS-485 systems run 10 kbps to 100 kbps; some reach 250 kbps over 4000 ft or more. Accepting 5 % to 10 % signal jitter allows longer runs. THVD1450, THVD1451 and THVD1452 run at 50 Mbps when the link is short, or loses little enough at the signal frequencies, to leave the data intact.
The stub between a transceiver and the trunk is an unterminated length of line, and its reflections vary in phase as it gets longer; the stub length equation gives its maximum.
The standard asks a driver to drive 32 unit loads, a unit load being about 12 kΩ. Each THVD14xx is 1/8 unit load, so up to 256 receivers can share a bus.

The IEC 61000-4-2 model stores its charge in 150 pF (charged through 50 MΩ) and discharges through 330 Ω; the HBM uses 100 pF (charged through 1 MΩ) and 1.5 kΩ. With 50 % more capacitance and 78 % less discharge resistance, the IEC test drives far higher discharge currents than HBM. IEC 61000-4-2 names contact discharge as its preferred test method.

EFT comes from relay contact bounce and from breaking inductive loads; surge from lightning, direct or induced, and from power-system switching, load changes and short circuits, typical of factory and grid equipment. A 0.5 kV surge or a 4 kV EFT carries far more pulse power than a 10 kV ESD event; 500 V surges are typical of factory automation, 6 kV surges of power generation and grid systems. Surge energy arrives as a long, slowly decaying pulse; dumped into the on-chip protection it turns to heat that can destroy the cells and the transceiver. The on-chip IEC protection is aimed at ESD; protection against longer-duration surge transients is added outside the part.

For 1 kV IEC 61000-4-5 surge, each bus line gets a 10 Ω pulse-proof thick-film resistor (Vishay CRCW0603010RJNEAHP) in series and a Bourns CDSOT23-SM712 bidirectional 400 W TVS to ground at the connector.

Every supply takes a 100 nF ceramic decoupling capacitor as near the supply pins as possible. It lowers ripple coming from switch-mode supplies and makes up for the resistance and inductance of the board's power planes.

Surge transients cover about 3 MHz to 300 MHz, so the board needs high-frequency layout practice. Protection parts sit next to the bus connector, in line with the signal path, so transient current is not forced to branch off to reach them. VCC and ground planes give low inductance; high-frequency current follows the lowest-impedance path. The transceiver, UART and controller each take 100 nF to 220 nF decoupling at their VCC pins. Decoupling capacitors and protection parts each get at least two vias to VCC and to ground. Enable lines carry 1 kΩ to 10 kΩ pull-ups or pull-downs, which limit noise current in them during transients. Pulse-proof series resistors in A and B, used when the TVS clamps above the bus pins' rating, limit the residual clamp current and prevent latch-up. TVS diodes alone cover surges up to 1 kV; higher surges need metal-oxide varistors, which bring the transient down to a few hundred volts, and transient blocking units, which keep the current under 1 mA.
Power-up and power-down are glitch-free, which allows hot plug-in.
The part shuts down at a junction temperature of 170 °C typical.
